prompt: The section splits the kinetic energy of two particles A and B into (P^2)/(2M) + (p^2)/(2μ), where P is the total momentum, p the relative momentum and μ the reduced mass. What do the two terms describe?

choices.text: Motion of A alone and motion of B alone
choices.why: That is the starting form, (p_A^2)/(2m_A) + (p_B^2)/(2m_B). The new terms use the total momentum P and the relative momentum p instead.

choices.text: Translation and rotation of the pair
choices.why: Both terms are translational kinetic energy. One is the motion of the pair as a whole, the other the motion of A and B relative to each other.

choices.text: Kinetic and potential energy of the pair
choices.why: No potential energy appears; both terms are kinetic. One belongs to the center of mass, the other to the relative motion.

explanation: With P = p_A + p_B and M = m_A + m_B, the first term is the kinetic energy of the pair moving as a whole. The second, with the reduced mass μ = (m_A m_B)/(m_A + m_B), is the energy of their relative motion, which is what matters in a collision.

prompt: The section defines the relative velocity of molecules A and B as v = v_A − v_B. If A and B close in on each other along a line with v_B = −v_A, how large is v?

choices.text: Twice the speed of either one

choices.why: They cancel only in the sum v_A + v_B. The relative velocity is the difference, v_A − (−v_A) = 2v_A.

choices.text: The same as the speed of either one
choices.why: Each moves at that speed relative to the container. Relative to each other they close in twice as fast: v = 2v_A.

choices.text: √2 times the speed of either one
choices.why: √2 links the mean relative speed to ⟨v⟩ after averaging over all the molecules. For a head-on approach the relative speed is exactly 2v_A.

explanation: The relative velocity is v = v_A − v_B. With v_B = −v_A this gives v = 2v_A, so the two molecules close the gap at twice the speed of either one.

prompt: The section calls the average kinetic energy of relative motion, ⟨(p^2)/(2μ)⟩, the collision energy. At the same temperature, how does it compare for a pair of H2 molecules and a pair of Xe atoms?

choices.text: Larger for Xe, the heavier pair
choices.why: Heavier atoms move more slowly. By equipartition the relative kinetic energy is (3/2)k_B T whatever the masses.

choices.text: Larger for H2, the faster pair
choices.why: H2 molecules move faster but are lighter. Equipartition gives (3/2)k_B T for the relative motion of any pair.
Two molecules carry 3k_B T together, but half of it is in the motion of the center of mass. The relative motion gets (3/2)k_B T.

explanation: Equipartition gives ⟨(p^2)/(2μ)⟩ = (3/2)k_B T for any pair. The section stresses that this is mass independent, so H2 pairs and Xe pairs collide with the same average energy at a given T.

prompt: Two identical spherical molecules each have diameter d. Why does the section draw a collision sphere of radius d, not d/2, around each one?

choices.text: At contact their centers are d apart

choices.why: The molecules are treated as hard spheres of fixed size. The radius is d because two centers are one diameter apart when the spheres touch.

choices.text: The areas of the two molecules add
choices.why: Adding two areas gives 2π(d/2)^2 = πd^2/2, only half of σ. A collision happens whenever the centers come within d, so σ = πd^2.

choices.text: It makes room for the molecules' speeds
choices.why: The collision sphere depends only on size, not on speed. Its radius is d because touching spheres have centers one diameter apart.

explanation: Two spheres of diameter d touch when their centers are d apart. So a molecule hits any other whose center comes within d of its own, and the target area is σ = πd^2, not π(d/2)^2.

prompt: A spherical molecule has diameter d = 0.30 nm. Using σ = πd^2, what is its collision cross-section, in nm^2? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: σ = π(0.30 nm)^2 = 3.1416 × 0.090 nm^2 = 0.283 nm^2. Using the radius instead, π(0.15 nm)^2, would give only a quarter of this, because the collision sphere has radius d.

prompt: Molecule A has diameter 0.30 nm and molecule B has diameter 0.50 nm. Using the section's d_AB = (1/2)(d_A + d_B), what effective diameter goes into σ_AB = πd_AB^2?

choices.why: That is d_A + d_B. At contact the centers are one radius of A plus one radius of B apart, which is the average of the diameters: 0.40 nm.
That is the geometric mean, √(0.30 × 0.50). The section uses the arithmetic mean, (0.30 + 0.50)/2 = 0.40 nm.
The larger diameter alone overstates the contact distance. The two centers meet at (0.30 + 0.50)/2 = 0.40 nm.

explanation: d_AB = (1/2)(0.30 nm + 0.50 nm) = 0.40 nm, the distance between the centers when A and B touch. The cross-section is then σ_AB = π(0.40 nm)^2 ≈ 0.50 nm^2.

prompt: A molecule with collision cross-section σ moves a distance l. Ignoring the rounded ends, what volume does its collision cylinder sweep out?

choices.why: ρσl is the number of molecules in the cylinder, so it counts collisions. The volume itself is σl.
That uses the molecule's own radius d/2. The cylinder's radius is the collision diameter d, so its base is σ = πd^2 and its volume σl.
Volume is base area times length, not area divided by length. The base is σ and the length l, so the volume is σl.

explanation: A cylinder's volume is its base area times its length: here σ = πd^2 times l. Multiplying by the number density ρ gives the number of collisions along the way, N_coll = ρσl.

prompt: A molecule sweeps out a collision cylinder whose radius is d, the molecular diameter. According to the section, which other molecules does it hit?

choices.text: Those with their center inside it
Any that even partly overlap it
choices.why: The radius d already allows for the size of both molecules. One that only partly overlaps the cylinder has its center more than d from the path and is missed.

choices.text: Only those lying right on its path
choices.why: A hit needs the centers to come within d, not to be lined up exactly. Any molecule whose center is inside the cylinder is hit.

choices.text: Only those lying wholly inside it
choices.why: A molecule can stick out of the cylinder and still be hit. Only its center needs to lie inside, within d of the path.

explanation: Two molecules touch when their centers are d apart. So a molecule is hit exactly when its center lies within d of the path, that is, inside the cylinder of radius d.

prompt: The section first finds z_A = ρσ⟨v⟩ for the collision frequency of one molecule, then corrects it to z_A = √2 ρσ⟨v⟩. Where does the √2 come from?

choices.why: Counting both partners matters for the total rate per volume, where it brings in a factor 1/2. The √2 comes from the motion of the targets: ⟨v_r⟩ = √2⟨v⟩.

choices.text: The cylinder's rounded ends add volume
choices.why: The ends were ignored. The √2 appears because the targets move, so the speed that counts is the mean relative speed ⟨v_r⟩ = √2⟨v⟩.
Shape would change σ, not add a √2. The factor comes from using the mean relative speed, ⟨v_r⟩ = √2⟨v⟩, because all molecules move.

explanation: z_A = ρσ⟨v⟩ assumes that only one molecule moves. With all of them moving, the speed that counts is the mean relative speed ⟨v_r⟩ = √((8k_B T)/(πμ)), and for identical molecules μ = m_A/2, so ⟨v_r⟩ = √2⟨v⟩.

prompt: z_A is the number of collisions that one molecule makes per second. What does its reciprocal, 1/z_A, measure?

choices.why: The mean free path is a distance, λ = ⟨v⟩/z_A. The reciprocal 1/z_A is a time: the average wait between collisions.

choices.text: The collisions per second in a unit volume
choices.why: That is Z_AA = (1/2)ρ z_A, which counts the collisions of all the molecules. 1/z_A is the average time between collisions of one molecule.

choices.text: The time to reach the container wall
choices.why: Wall collisions have their own rate. 1/z_A is the average time between collisions with other molecules.

explanation: If a molecule collides z_A times per second, the average time between its collisions is 1/z_A. Multiplying this time by the mean speed ⟨v⟩ gives the mean free path.

prompt: The mean free path is λ = ⟨v⟩/z_A, the mean speed times the average time between collisions. A molecule has ⟨v⟩ = 480 m/s and λ = 6.0 × 10^−8 m. How many collisions does it make per second, z_A, in s^−1? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e9.)
explanation: z_A = ⟨v⟩/λ = (480 m/s)/(6.0 × 10^−8 m) = 8.0 × 10^9 s^−1. Its reciprocal, 1.25 × 10^−10 s, is the average time between collisions.

prompt: What is the mean free path λ of a gas molecule?

choices.text: Average distance it travels between collisions

choices.why: The spacing of the molecules is a different quantity. λ is how far a molecule travels, on average, from one collision to the next.

choices.text: Average distance it travels before hitting a wall
choices.why: λ concerns collisions with other molecules. It is the average distance a molecule covers between two such collisions.
That radius is d, the molecular diameter. λ is the average distance traveled between collisions, λ = 1/(√2 ρσ).

explanation: The section defines λ as the average distance a molecule travels between collisions: its mean speed ⟨v⟩ times the average time between collisions, 1/z_A. This gives λ = 1/(√2 ρσ).

prompt: Example 27.6.1 uses H2 at 1.00 bar and 298 K, where ρ = 2.43 × 10^25 m^−3 and σ = 2.30 × 10^−19 m^2. Using λ = 1/(√2 ρσ), what is the mean free path of H2, in nm? (Give it as a decimal.)
At 298 K and 1.0 bar, a gas has a mean free path of 66 nm. Using λ = (RT)/(√2 N_A σ P), what is λ at 2.0 bar and the same temperature, in nm?
explanation: At fixed T, λ is inversely proportional to P: doubling the pressure doubles the number density, so a molecule meets another twice as soon. λ = 66 nm/2 = 33 nm.

prompt: The section writes λ = (RT)/(√2 N_A σ P). At constant pressure, what happens to λ when the temperature rises from 300 K to 600 K?

choices.why: T sits in the numerator of λ = (RT)/(√2 N_A σ P). At fixed P, doubling T halves the number density, so λ doubles.
√2 would follow if λ went as the mean speed, which goes as √T. λ goes as 1/ρ, and at fixed P the density halves when T doubles.
Faster molecules collide more often, but they also travel farther, so the speed cancels. At fixed P, λ is proportional to T.

explanation: At constant P, λ = (RT)/(√2 N_A σ P) is proportional to T. Doubling T from 300 K to 600 K halves the number density ρ = (P N_A)/(RT), so λ doubles.

prompt: A gas in a closed steel tank is warmed from 300 K to 600 K. The tank keeps the number density ρ fixed. What happens to the mean free path λ?

choices.text: It doubles, since λ is proportional to T
choices.why: λ ∝ T holds at constant pressure, where the gas expands. In a closed tank ρ is fixed, so λ = 1/(√2 ρσ) does not change.

choices.text: It shrinks, as faster molecules collide more
choices.why: They do collide more often, but they also move farther between collisions. The two effects cancel, leaving λ = 1/(√2 ρσ) unchanged.

choices.text: It grows by √2, like the mean speed
choices.why: The speed cancels out of λ = ⟨v⟩/z_A. With ρ and σ fixed, λ = 1/(√2 ρσ) is unchanged.

explanation: λ = 1/(√2 ρσ) depends only on the number density and the cross-section. Warming a closed tank raises the pressure and the speeds, but ρ and σ stay the same, so λ does too.

prompt: Gas X and gas Y are at the same temperature and pressure, but the molecules of X have twice the diameter of those of Y. How does λ for X compare with λ for Y?

choices.why: λ goes as 1/σ, and σ = πd^2 grows as the square of the diameter. Doubling d makes σ four times larger, so λ is a quarter as long.
That would follow if λ went as 1/d^3, like a volume. λ depends on the area σ = πd^2, so doubling d gives a quarter.
Bigger molecules make a bigger target, so collisions come sooner. With σ four times larger, λ = 1/(√2 ρσ) is a quarter as long.

explanation: At the same T and P the two gases have the same number density ρ. Doubling d multiplies σ = πd^2 by 4, so λ = 1/(√2 ρσ) becomes a quarter as long.

prompt: The section gives λ = (RT)/(√2 N_A σ P), with R = 8.314 J K^−1 mol^−1 and N_A = 6.022 × 10^23 mol^−1. For a gas with σ = 4.0 × 10^−19 m^2 at 300 K and a low pressure of 1.0 Pa, what is λ, in mm? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: λ = (8.314 × 300)/(1.414 × 6.022 × 10^23 × 4.0 × 10^−19 × 1.0) m = 2494/(3.41 × 10^5) m = 7.32 × 10^−3 m = 7.32 mm. At 1 bar the same gas has λ ≈ 73 nm, so at this low pressure λ is about 10^5 times longer.

prompt: Why does a molecule in a gas follow a zigzag, random-walk path?

choices.why: The molecule moves in a straight line between collisions. Its direction changes at each collision, at random times and in random ways.
Vibration does not steer the molecule. Its direction changes when it collides with other molecules or with the walls.
Gravity plays no part in the section's picture. The zigzags come from collisions with other molecules and with the walls.

explanation: Every collision with another molecule or a wall sends the molecule off in a new direction. Since the collisions happen at random times and in random ways, the path looks like a random walk.

prompt: In the section's one-dimensional random walk, a molecule takes N steps of length λ, each one randomly to the right or to the left. Why does it usually end up much closer to its start than Nλ?

choices.text: Steps right and left largely cancel
Its steps get shorter as it slows down
choices.why: Every step has the same length λ in this model. The net distance is small because right and left steps mostly cancel.

choices.text: It always returns to its starting point
choices.why: It does not return exactly; it ends a net (i − j)λ away. That is much less than Nλ because right and left steps largely cancel.

choices.text: Most of its steps are to the left
choices.why: Left and right are equally likely, like heads and tails. Because they come in roughly equal numbers, they largely cancel.

explanation: With i steps to the right and j to the left, the net displacement is (i − j)λ, while the path length is Nλ. Since right and left are equally likely, i and j are close, and the typical distance is only about √N λ.

prompt: For a random walk of N steps of length λ, the section's distribution of net distances has width L = √N λ. A molecule with λ = 60 nm makes N = 400 collisions. What is L, in nm?
explanation: √400 = 20, so L = 20 × 60 nm = 1200 nm. The total path is Nλ = 24,000 nm, but the steps largely cancel, so the typical net distance is far shorter.

prompt: The number of collisions grows with time as N = z_A t, and a random walk spreads over a distance L = √N λ. How much longer must you wait for L to double?

choices.why: L grows as √N, not as N. Doubling L needs four times as many steps, and so four times the time.
Since L ∝ √t, the time must grow by the square of the distance factor. Doubling L takes 2^2 = 4 times as long.
That would hold if L went as the cube root of t. With L ∝ √t, doubling L needs 2^2 = 4 times the time.

explanation: L = √N λ = √(z_A t) λ, so L grows as √t. To double L, t must grow by a factor of 2^2 = 4: a random walk spreads quickly at first and then more and more slowly.

prompt: For a large number of steps N, what shape does the section find for the probability P(k) that a one-dimensional random walk ends k steps to the right of its start?

choices.text: A flat line, every k equally likely
choices.why: Far more step sequences end near the start than far from it. P(k) ∝ exp(−(k^2)/(2N)) is a bell curve peaked at k = 0.

choices.text: A Gaussian centered at k = N/2
choices.why: Right and left steps are equally likely, so on average they cancel and the peak is at k = 0. P(k) ∝ exp(−(k^2)/(2N)).

choices.text: A curve peaked at k = N
choices.why: k = N needs every step to go right, the least likely outcome. The most likely net result is k = 0.

explanation: Counting the ways to get i heads and j tails and using Stirling's approximation gives P(k) ∝ exp(−(k^2)/(2N)). This Gaussian peaks at k = 0, and its width grows as √N.

prompt: The section defines the diffusion constant as D = z_A λ^2/2. What units does D have?

choices.why: That would be a volume per time. λ^2 is an area, in m^2, and z_A is in s^−1, so D is in m^2 s^−1.
λ^2 alone is an area, but it is multiplied by the collision frequency z_A, in s^−1. So D has units of m^2 s^−1.
That is the unit of z_A alone. Multiplying by λ^2 adds m^2, giving m^2 s^−1.

explanation: z_A is a frequency (s^−1) and λ^2 an area (m^2), so D = z_A λ^2/2 has units of m^2 s^−1. As the section notes, that is a length squared per unit time.

prompt: For a gas of only A molecules, the section writes Z_AA = (1/2)ρ z_A for the total number of collisions per unit volume per second. Why the factor 1/2?

choices.text: ρ z_A counts each collision twice
Only half the molecules are moving
choices.why: All the molecules move. The 1/2 is there because ρ z_A counts each A–A collision once for each of its two partners.

choices.text: It averages the two partners' speeds
choices.why: Speeds enter through ⟨v_r⟩, inside z_A. The 1/2 removes double counting: ρ z_A counts each collision once per partner.
The √2 survives: Z_AA = σ⟨v⟩ρ^2/√2. The 1/2 is there because each A–A collision would otherwise be counted twice.

explanation: ρ z_A adds up the collisions of every molecule, but each A–A collision involves two molecules and so would be counted twice. The section compares this with rolling a double 3 with two dice: there is only one way to do it.

prompt: At a fixed temperature, the number density ρ of a pure gas is doubled. By what factor does the total collision frequency per unit volume, Z_AA = σ⟨v⟩ρ^2/√2, change?

choices.why: Each molecule's own rate z_A doubles, but there are also twice as many molecules per volume. Z_AA goes as ρ^2, so it rises fourfold.
The √2 in Z_AA is a fixed number from the relative speed. Doubling ρ multiplies ρ^2 by 4.
More molecules per volume means more collisions, both per molecule and in total. Z_AA ∝ ρ^2 rises fourfold.

explanation: Z_AA = (1/2)ρ z_A, and z_A itself is proportional to ρ, so Z_AA ∝ ρ^2. Doubling ρ at fixed T leaves σ and ⟨v⟩ alone and multiplies Z_AA by 2^2 = 4.

prompt: A pure gas has number density ρ = 2.0 × 10^25 m^−3, and each molecule collides z_A = 6.0 × 10^9 times per second. Using Z_AA = (1/2)ρ z_A, what is the total number of collisions per cubic meter per second, in s^−1 m^−3? (Type it in scientific notation, like 2.5e34.)
explanation: Z_AA = (1/2)(2.0 × 10^25 m^−3)(6.0 × 10^9 s^−1) = 6.0 × 10^34 s^−1 m^−3. The 1/2 is needed because ρ z_A counts every collision once for each of its two partners.

prompt: Example 27.6.1 finds Z = 1.7 × 10^35 s^−1 m^−3 for H2–H2 collisions at 1.00 bar and 298 K. Since 1 m^3 = 10^6 cm^3, what is this per cubic centimeter?

choices.why: That divides by 100, which converts a length, not a volume. A cubic meter holds 10^6 cm^3, so divide by 10^6.
A cubic centimeter is smaller than a cubic meter, so it holds fewer collisions. Divide by 10^6; do not multiply.
The number must change with the size of the unit volume. Each cm^3 is 10^−6 m^3, so it has 10^−6 as many collisions.

explanation: Each cubic centimeter is 10^−6 m^3, so it holds 10^−6 as many collisions: 1.7 × 10^35 × 10^−6 = 1.7 × 10^29 s^−1 cm^−3, the example's final answer. That is still about 10^29 collisions every second in 1 cm^3 of H2.
